# ![[Uncaptioned image]](2609.39765v1/figures/memdgm_emblem.png) MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents

Xiaoqiang Wang    Bang Liu Affiliation: \[ Affiliation: \[
Email: <bang.liu@umontreal.ca>

September 30, 2026

###### Abstract

Agent memory faces heterogeneous access needs: a single-hop question may
require one piece of evidence, whereas a multi-hop question must combine
evidence from multiple sources. Predefined memory workflows cannot adapt
to these varying needs. Recent adaptive methods search or learn over
memory components and their compositions, but the design space itself
remains predefined. We introduce MemCodex, a self-evolving hierarchical
memory system that organizes experience into executable memory programs
for summaries, relational knowledge, reusable skills, and latent memory.
Open-ended program evolution searches the open design space of layer
programs by rewriting how each layer is constructed, indexed, retrieved,
and routed, thereby adapting both within-layer implementations and
cross-layer composition. At query time, reads traverse the hierarchy
from coarse to fine and stop once sufficient evidence is found,
descending to the original history when needed. We further develop
MemArena, a unified runtime that places heterogeneous data and memory
systems behind a common interface. MemCodex improves average task
success by $`10.1\%`$ relative to the strongest adaptive-memory
baseline, with $`3.4\times`$ fewer context tokens and $`2.1\times`$
faster inference.

## 1 Introduction

Language agents \[[72](#bib.bib72), [53](#bib.bib53), [30](#bib.bib30),
[5](#bib.bib5)\] increasingly act over long horizons in web
navigation \[[83](#bib.bib83)\], software
engineering \[[22](#bib.bib22), [12](#bib.bib12)\] and computer
use \[[68](#bib.bib68), [54](#bib.bib54)\], and self-evolve from
experience \[[51](#bib.bib51)\] through reflection on
failures \[[48](#bib.bib48)\], skill accumulation \[[52](#bib.bib52),
[80](#bib.bib80), [39](#bib.bib39), [47](#bib.bib47)\] and code
rewriting \[[76](#bib.bib76)\]. Across sessions, much of this experience
survives only in memory. Hand-designed pipelines organize it through
rolling summaries in systems such as MemoryBank and
MemGPT \[[82](#bib.bib82), [40](#bib.bib40)\], facts and entity
graphs \[[71](#bib.bib71), [42](#bib.bib42), [8](#bib.bib8)\], skill
stores \[[80](#bib.bib80), [39](#bib.bib39), [52](#bib.bib52)\], or
memory written into parameters or latent state \[[59](#bib.bib59),
[1](#bib.bib1), [26](#bib.bib26), [56](#bib.bib56)\]. Yet these
pipelines face _access heterogeneity_, because the memory organization a
query needs depends on the query, the record and the
task \[[70](#bib.bib70), [35](#bib.bib35), [17](#bib.bib17)\]. This
heterogeneity appears across query types, since single-hop questions
need raw turns \[[11](#bib.bib11)\], multi-hop questions need
cross-session links \[[10](#bib.bib10)\], temporal questions need dated
events \[[9](#bib.bib9)\], and repeated procedures need
skills \[[62](#bib.bib62)\]. Adaptive computation in reasoning shows the
same pattern, where dynamic shortcuts spend depth only on the steps that
need it \[[58](#bib.bib58)\]. A hand-designed pipeline hard-codes both
which organizations exist and the rule that chooses among them, and a
study of fourteen memory systems \[[84](#bib.bib84)\] finds that no
architecture dominates across tasks.

Adaptive memory addresses this rigidity in two main directions. One
direction searches a predefined design space by selecting and composing
modules for encoding, storage, retrieval, and
management \[[6](#bib.bib6), [35](#bib.bib35), [74](#bib.bib74)\]. The
other, exemplified by Mem-alpha, learns policies for when and how to
write, update, and retrieve memory \[[60](#bib.bib60), [57](#bib.bib57),
[50](#bib.bib50), [61](#bib.bib61)\]. Despite their different forms,
both directions must jointly determine _how_ experience is organized
into memory and _how_ queries access it, since retrieval can only use
structures created during writing. As shown in ![[Uncaptioned
image]](2609.39765v1/figures/memdgm_emblem.png) MemCodex:
Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents, this coupling
places memory systems along two axes: memory organization and design
search. Among prior systems, only MemPro \[[34](#bib.bib34)\] opens the
design itself to program search, but it evolves a single monolithic
program over flat memory, without a hierarchy whose components can
evolve and be accessed independently.

![Refer to caption](2609.39765v1/fig2_arch.png)

Figure 1: MemCodex workflow. In the task loop (upper), MemArena writes
the record and poses each query $`q`$ to the task agent, which reads a
context $`C`$ from the layer hierarchy, stopping at the coarsest
sufficient layer or descending to source turns, and answers $`a`$. In
the program evolution loop (lower), run once per round, a parent is
sampled from the archive of architectures $`g=(\lambda,\psi)`$, meta
agent $`\rho`$ rewrites one method of one layer program $`\psi_{\ell}`$,
and validity checks and the acceptance test decide whether the child
enters the archive.

We therefore introduce MemCodex, a hierarchical memory system whose
layers are executable memory programs behind a fixed interface and
runtime. Program evolution adapts both the write and read code of
individual layers and their cross-layer composition, that is, which
layers are active and how items and reads pass between them. Within this
hierarchy, MemCodex organizes skill, graph, and summary above an
append-only raw layer, with kv memory providing latent memory.

Inspired by the Darwin Gödel Machine \[[76](#bib.bib76)\] and
HyperAgents \[[77](#bib.bib77)\], which evolve an agent by rewriting its
own code, we apply program evolution to this memory hierarchy. At each
round, a meta agent draws a parent from the archive and rewrites one
method of one layer or toggles one layer. Restricting each child to one
change makes the effect of that change attributable. An acceptance test
then keeps changes that improve accuracy or reduce token use without
degrading the other, and accuracy-only gains must additionally pass a
one-sided McNemar test \[[37](#bib.bib37)\]. Before this test, validity
checks $`\mathcal{K}`$ reject changes that break the memory constraints.

The fixed interface exposes five methods in each layer, spanning both
memory writing and reading. On the write side, $`\mathrm{admit}`$
filters candidates, $`\mathrm{index}`$ keeps a bounded active set, and
$`\mathrm{propose}`$ derives items for the layer above. On the read
side, $`\mathrm{score}`$ ranks candidates and $`\mathrm{route}`$ decides
where the search proceeds next. Reads move from coarse to fine layers,
with $`\mathrm{route}`$ choosing Stop, Narrow, or Descend until
sufficient evidence is found or the search reaches the raw history.
Because every stored item retains its exact source turns, the original
evidence remains recoverable even after lossy summarization.

To evaluate these mechanisms systematically across diverse sources,
interaction formats, and evaluation protocols, we further develop
MemArena, a heterogeneous agent-source evaluation suite with a unified
data interface, access interface, and metric suite covering benchmarks
such as LoCoMo \[[36](#bib.bib36)\], LongMemEval
(LME) \[[63](#bib.bib63)\], and MemoryAgentBench
(MAB) \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. It separates the memory system from the task
agent, as capability-level evaluation dissociates what a language model
knows from how it reasons \[[55](#bib.bib55)\]. Under one protocol,
MemArena spans seven sources, eleven baseline systems and two backbones,
while each new source requires only one adapter. Under this evaluation,
MemCodex gains $`5.6`$ average accuracy points over the strongest
baseline with Qwen3.5-27B \[[41](#bib.bib41)\] and $`3.6`$ with the API
model GPT-5.4-mini, while reading $`3.4\times`$ fewer tokens and
answering $`2.1\times`$ faster.

## 2 MemCodex: Hierarchical Memory as Evolving Programs

We model agent memory as a hierarchy of executable memory programs whose
implementations and composition evolve with the task
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")).
A fixed five-method layer interface and runtime constrain how these
programs interact while leaving their internal behavior open to
evolution.

We model long-horizon memory as a task agent $`\pi`$ answering questions
about a record $`R`$ that arrives as write chunks $`R_{1},\dots,R_{n}`$
of timestamped turns $`v`$, where each question $`q`$ is posed once the
record up to its question time has been written. A memory system with
architecture $`g`$ keeps a store $`\mathcal{M}`$ and serves $`\pi`$
through a write operation and a read operation:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{M}\leftarrow\texttt{write}_{g}(\mathcal{M},R_{i}),\qquad C=\texttt{read}_{g}(\mathcal{M},q),\qquad a=\pi(q,C).
``` |  | (1) |

The write operation folds each chunk into the store, the read operation
returns a context $`C`$ of at most $`B`$ tokens, and $`\pi`$ answers
from the question and that context. To preserve exact evidence despite
this bounded context, the store contains an append-only *raw layer*
$`\mathcal{V}`$ of all turns and lossy *derived items* $`x`$ above it,
each of which retains its exact *source turns*
$`\mathrm{src}(x)\subseteq\mathcal{V}`$.

We represent each *architecture* as $`g=(\lambda,\psi)`$ with two parts.
The layer programs $`\psi`$ implement the write and the read through
five methods per layer. Specifically, the write operation uses
$`\mathrm{admit}`$, $`\mathrm{index}`$ and $`\mathrm{propose}`$, while
the read operation uses $`\mathrm{score}`$ and $`\mathrm{route}`$. The
layer mask $`\lambda`$ independently switches derived layers on or off.
For the questions $`\mathcal{Q}`$ of a task, each query $`q`$ has *gold
turns* $`G(q)\subseteq\mathcal{V}`$. The accuracy of $`g`$ is
$`\mathrm{acc}(g)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}}\,\mathbf{1}[\pi(q,C_{g}(q))\text{ correct}]`$
and its cost is
$`\mathrm{tok/q}(g)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}}|C_{g}(q)|`$. Our
objective is the most accurate architecture at no higher token cost than
$`g_{0}`$. We first define the layer programs $`\psi`$ and the read and
write operations they implement. We then define program evolution, which
changes $`g`$ one method rewrite or one layer toggle at a time and keeps
accepted architectures in an archive.

### 2.1 Layer Programs $`\psi`$

#### Layers.

Queries require different levels of abstraction, but every derived item
must remain connected to the raw evidence from which it was produced. We
therefore order the four text layers
$`\mathcal{L}=(\textsc{skill},\textsc{graph},\textsc{summary},\textsc{raw})`$
from coarse to fine, as in RAPTOR \[[44](#bib.bib44)\], with store
$`\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{V}\cup\bigcup_{\ell\neq\textsc{raw}}\mathcal{M}_{\ell}`$,
where $`\mathcal{M}_{\ell}`$ holds the derived items of layer $`\ell`$.
The raw layer keeps every raw turn $`v\in\mathcal{V}`$ unchanged so that
the original evidence remains available. The summary layer condenses
each closed segment of raw turns into a compact account of that segment.
The graph layer stores timed assertions $`x=(h,r,t,\tau)`$ extracted
from summaries, where entities $`h`$ and $`t`$ are linked by relation
$`r`$ over the time $`\tau`$ for which the relation holds, so that a
newer assertion can supersede an older one about the same entities. The
skill layer stores executable procedures distilled from assertions that
record the same procedure in several sessions. We model a skill as a
program rather than a text note because a procedure that runs can be
checked against the sessions that demonstrate it. Each derived item
$`x`$ is built from inputs $`\mathrm{in}(x)`$ in the layer directly
below, and its exact source turns $`\mathrm{src}(x)`$ resolve
recursively,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{src}(v)=\{v\}\ \ (v\in\mathcal{V}),\qquad\mathrm{src}(x)=\textstyle\bigcup_{y\in\mathrm{in}(x)}\mathrm{src}(y)\ \ (x\in\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathcal{V}).
``` |  | (2) |

A read can therefore reach the raw turns underlying an assertion or a
skill without traversing its derivation. The set $`\mathrm{src}(x)`$
records the exact derivation of an item rather than a minimal evidence
set. In particular, a summary and its extracted assertions share the
segment’s turns, which Narrow and the raw-layer read subsequently
refine.

#### Layer interface.

Local program evolution requires every method rewrite to remain within
its target layer. We therefore expose each text layer through five
methods with distinct functionalities. Within a layer,
$`\mathrm{admit}_{\ell}`$ filters proposals, while
$`\mathrm{index}_{\ell}`$ retains at most $`K_{\ell}`$ items in the
active index $`\mathcal{I}_{\ell}`$. Evicted items remain in the store.
The method $`\mathrm{score}_{\ell}(q,S)`$ ranks the items $`S`$ allowed
by the *search scope* $`F\subseteq\mathcal{V}`$ and returns the top
candidate $`x^{\star}`$ with confidence $`c`$. Across layers,
$`\mathrm{propose}_{\ell}`$ sends derived items upward, while
$`\mathrm{route}_{\ell}(q,x^{\star},c)`$ returns Stop, Narrow or
Descend. The runtime owns assemble, which packs $`C`$ under $`B`$. In
every architecture, turns are appended only to the raw layer and never
changed. Every derived item names the exact raw turns used to build it.
Narrow can only restrict the search scope to the top candidate’s source
turns, $`F\cap\mathrm{src}(x^{\star})`$. Every context must also fit
within $`B`$ tokens. These four *memory constraints* ensure that any
read can trace a derived item back to raw turns, however lossy the item
is.

![Refer to caption](2609.39765v1/fig_channels.png)

Figure 2: Content and routing channels of MemCodex for a question about
Caroline. $`\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{txt}}`$ places summary $`x`$ in $`C`$,
omitting Paris, while $`\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{route}}`$ follows
$`\mathrm{src}(x)`$ to the raw turn naming Paris.

#### Content channel and routing channel.

A derived item can serve a query through two distinct channels, and the
query-adaptive read uses the routing channel. The channel is an
architecture setting rather than a per-query choice, so only the read
depth adapts to each query. In the *content channel*
$`\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{txt}}`$, the text of the top-scoring items enters
$`C`$ in place of their evidence, as in summary, profile and skill
memories \[[40](#bib.bib40), [4](#bib.bib4), [80](#bib.bib80)\]. In the
*routing channel* $`\mathsf{C}_{\mathrm{route}}`$, a retrieval hit leads
to its source turns, as HippoRAG passes node probability to source
passages \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. In the Caroline example of
[Figure 2](#S2.F2 "In Layer interface. ‣ 2.1 Layer Programs 𝜓 ‣ 2 MemCodex: Hierarchical Memory as Evolving Programs ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"),
the summary omits Paris, but routing through $`\mathrm{src}(x)`$
recovers the raw turn that names it. *Evidence preservation*, retaining
every derived item’s exact source turns, keeps this route available.

#### Query-adaptive read.

A fixed read depth can either skip useful abstractions or retrieve
unnecessary detail. The $`\texttt{read}_{g}`$ operation in
[Equation 1](#S2.E1 "In 2 MemCodex: Hierarchical Memory as Evolving Programs ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")
therefore visits layers from coarse to fine
([Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Latent memory. ‣ 2.1 Layer Programs 𝜓 ‣ 2 MemCodex: Hierarchical Memory as Evolving Programs ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"))
and lets each $`\mathrm{route}`$ determine whether traversal should
continue. Only Stop ends the read and adds the in-scope source turns
$`\mathrm{src}(x^{\star})\cap F`$ to $`C`$ in temporal order through the
routing channel. The Narrow action restricts the search scope to those
source turns, while Descend preserves the current scope, and both
actions continue to the next layer. At the raw layer, the $`k`$
highest-scoring in-scope turns enter $`C`$. The routing channel
therefore ensures that the task agent always answers from raw turns,
even when the read stops at a skill whose source turns are the sessions
that demonstrate the procedure. Each query consequently incurs only the
read depth it needs.

#### Write path.

Derived layers depend on lower-layer content, so the
$`\texttt{write}_{g}`$ operation in
[Equation 1](#S2.E1 "In 2 MemCodex: Hierarchical Memory as Evolving Programs ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")
processes each appended chunk from bottom to top through
$`\mathrm{propose}`$, $`\mathrm{admit}`$ and $`\mathrm{index}`$. Each
proposal to a layer combines the items newly admitted one layer below
for the current chunk with the active items of that lower layer. The
runtime records every item read to form the proposal as an input. At
skill, $`\mathrm{admit}`$ accepts a procedure only when replay on every
demonstration session reproduces the recorded outcome. The task agent’s
backbone writes the textual proposals. In the initial architecture
$`g_{0}`$, $`\mathrm{index}`$ retains items according to the
access-and-recency heat of MemoryOS \[[23](#bib.bib23)\],
$`\mathrm{score}`$ uses cosine similarity and $`\mathrm{route}`$ stops
or narrows above per-layer thresholds.

#### Latent memory.

Some associations in the record have no representation in any text
layer. We feed each write chunk into Metis-27B \[[79](#bib.bib79)\], a
memory foundation model with stateful fast weights, and use the state of
its memory blocks as kv memory, a fixed-size key-value memory. kv memory
is write-only, exposes no score or route, is built on the write path,
and is not evolved. Two interfaces provide memory to the task agent. The
natural language (NL) interface places the text context $`C`$ in the
prompt and supports any agent. The KV interface injects kv memory into
an open-weight agent’s memory attention. Because an API agent exposes
neither weights nor activations, it uses only the NL interface and has
no latent memory.

Algorithm 2 ProgramEvolution

### 2.2 Evolving the Architecture $`g`$

#### Architecture.

Joint evolution of layer behavior and composition requires each edit to
remain local to one component. The layer mask
$`\lambda\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{L}|-1}`$ covers the derived layers, while
the raw layer remains active. Reads visit only the active layers. Writes
run through every layer up to the highest active one so that every
proposal retains its type and derivation, including when an intermediate
layer is switched off for reading. The layer mask and cross-layer
methods determine composition, while the within-layer methods determine
implementation. Starting from $`g_{0}`$, program evolution combines
evaluator-guided program search \[[14](#bib.bib14), [43](#bib.bib43),
[38](#bib.bib38)\], the archive-based open-ended search of the Darwin
Gödel Machine \[[76](#bib.bib76)\] and the meta agent of
HyperAgents \[[77](#bib.bib77)\]. Meta agent $`\rho`$ runs on the task
agent’s backbone, so the agent programs its own memory. *Attributable
edits* restrict every child to one method rewrite of one layer or one
layer toggle, so each accepted change traces to one edit. The acceptance
test then accepts only improvements that do not trade accuracy against
token cost.

#### Archive.

A single chain of edits cannot recover after reaching a dead end.
Following MemPro \[[34](#bib.bib34)\], we therefore store accepted
architectures in the archive $`\mathcal{A}`$, which forms a tree, while
rejected children enter their parent’s rejection log
$`\mathcal{J}_{n}`$. Each node stores evolve-question accuracy
$`\mathrm{acc}_{Q}`$, tokens per question and verdicts
$`\mathbf{v}_{g}\in\{0,1\}^{|Q|}`$. A parent is drawn with probability
proportional to

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w(n)=\sigma\!\Big(\tfrac{\mathrm{acc}_{Q}(g_{n})-\overline{\mathrm{acc}}}{\hat{\sigma}}\Big)\cdot\frac{1}{1+|\mathrm{ch}(n)|}\cdot(1+d_{n}),
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\sigma`$ is logistic, $`\overline{\mathrm{acc}}`$ and
$`\hat{\sigma}`$ are the archive accuracy mean and spread,
$`\mathrm{ch}(n)`$ the children of $`n`$ and $`d_{n}`$ its normalized
crowding distance on the accuracy-cost Pareto front (zero off it), so
the weight favors accurate, rarely expanded nodes on the front. Any
archived architecture can become a parent, and a child may contain any
code that satisfies the layer interface. Program evolution therefore
remains open-ended rather than following a single chain of edits.

#### Self-modification.

Each local edit should address an observed failure. The parent’s
diagnosis $`\mathcal{D}(g)`$ therefore examines failed traces and
refused or evicted items, then assigns each failure to the first method
that loses a gold turn. Children target successive methods or layer
toggles according to fault count, so siblings make distinct edits. For a
method rewrite, meta agent $`\rho`$ reads the target layer’s code,
diagnosis and rejection log, then returns a subclass that overrides only
that method
([Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Latent memory. ‣ 2.1 Layer Programs 𝜓 ‣ 2 MemCodex: Hierarchical Memory as Evolving Programs ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")).
Validity checks $`\mathcal{K}`$ reject any child that violates a memory
constraint on fixture queries.

#### Acceptance test.

Validity checks determine whether a child preserves the memory
constraints, but they do not determine whether it trades accuracy for
token cost. The acceptance test therefore compares child and parent on
the same evolve questions with the task agent and judge frozen,
accepting the child exactly when

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathsf{Accept}(g\to g^{\prime})\iff\Delta_{\mathrm{tok}}\leq 0\ \wedge\ \Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}\geq 0\ \wedge\ \big[(\Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}>0\ \wedge\ p<\alpha)\ \vee\ \Delta_{\mathrm{tok}}<0\big],
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}`$ and $`\Delta_{\mathrm{tok}}`$ are
child-minus-parent changes in accuracy and tokens per question, $`p`$ is
the one-sided exact McNemar $`p`$-value \[[37](#bib.bib37)\] on
discordant pairs of $`\mathbf{v}_{g}`$ and $`\mathbf{v}_{g^{\prime}}`$,
and $`\alpha=0.05`$. The evolved architecture $`g^{\star}`$ is the
archived architecture with the highest evolve-split accuracy.

## 3 MemArena: A Heterogeneous Agent-Source Evaluation Suite

![Refer to caption](2609.39765v1/fig_arena.png)

Figure 3: The MemArena evaluation suite, with heterogeneous sources
behind unified data and access interfaces and a metric suite.

Memory systems are reported on sources with different evidence formats,
time representations and access protocols, so their results are
difficult to compare directly. MemArena addresses this problem by
placing heterogeneous sources and memory systems behind one data
interface, one access interface and one metric suite, which allows any
memory module to be evaluated with any task agent under a fixed backbone
and judge. It currently spans seven sources, eleven baseline systems and
two backbones. We release the suite together with its adapters and
wrappers.

#### Data interface.

Source adapters map corpora with different evidence and time
representations into an episode $`e=(R,\mathcal{Q}_{e})`$
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3 MemArena: A Heterogeneous Agent-Source Evaluation Suite ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")).
The record $`R`$ orders sessions of timestamped, speaker-tagged turns,
while each tuple $`(q,a^{\star},G(q),y_{q},t_{q})\in\mathcal{Q}_{e}`$
specifies a question, reference answer, gold turns, question type and
question time, posed after the record through $`t_{q}`$ is written.
Source adapters obtain $`G(q)`$ from evidence annotations for LoCoMo and
LongMemEval and from task construction for PersonaMind and MAB. They
cover seven sources \[[36](#bib.bib36), [63](#bib.bib63),
[15](#bib.bib15), [20](#bib.bib20), [27](#bib.bib27), [7](#bib.bib7),
[81](#bib.bib81)\], and adding a source requires only a source adapter.
PersonaMind, our fourth benchmark, poses five preference or procedure
questions for each of 300 PersonaMem-V2 and InMind records, yielding
1,500 questions.

#### Access interface.

To separate memory quality from task-agent quality, MemArena wraps
memory systems and task agents independently. A memory wrapper exposes
$`\texttt{write}(\mathcal{M},R_{i})\to\mathcal{M}^{\prime}`$ and
$`\texttt{read}(\mathcal{M},q)\to C`$, where $`C`$ may carry kv memory.
An agent wrapper separately exposes $`\texttt{answer}(q,C)\to a`$ for
task agent $`\pi`$, using the NL interface for text and, for open-weight
agents, the KV interface for kv memory. The harness writes each record
into a fresh store in 20-turn chunks and poses each question after the
last chunk written before $`t_{q}`$, so stores are never shared across
records or users and only $`g`$ is shared. This separation allows any
task agent to be evaluated with any memory module. Within each
comparison, the harness fixes the backbone and judge, so systems differ
only in memory.

#### Metric suite.

MemArena measures both task success and memory cost. Accuracy
$`\mathrm{acc}`$ is the judge verdict on $`a`$ against $`a^{\star}`$
under the Mem0 rubric \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Where gold turns are
annotated, evidence recall is
$`\mathrm{Rec}=\mathbb{E}_{q}[|G(q)\cap C|/|G(q)|]`$. Context cost
$`\mathrm{tok/q}`$ counts prompt tokens per question, and inference time
measures wall-clock latency from read to the last answer token.

## 4 Experiments

#### Benchmarks and splits.

We evaluate every system through MemArena on
LoCoMo \[[36](#bib.bib36)\], LongMemEval (S split) \[[63](#bib.bib63)\],
MemoryAgentBench (MAB) \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] and PersonaMind. Following
MemEvolve \[[74](#bib.bib74)\] and MemPro \[[34](#bib.bib34)\], which
evolve on a held-out slice of each benchmark, we take 20 percent of each
benchmark’s questions as the evolve split $`Q`$. We stratify $`Q`$ by
question category, such as single-hop, multi-hop, temporal and
open-domain questions on LoCoMo, the five abilities of LongMemEval, the
four competencies of MAB, and preference against procedure questions on
PersonaMind. We never read the test split during search.

#### Baselines.

Unstructured baselines are 32k-token full context and dense RAG with
BGE \[[67](#bib.bib67)\] over 512-token chunks under $`B=4{,}096`$.
Hand-designed baselines are MemGPT \[[40](#bib.bib40)\],
A-Mem \[[71](#bib.bib71)\], Mem0 \[[4](#bib.bib4)\],
MemoryOS \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] and HMO \[[33](#bib.bib33)\]. Adaptive or
evolved baselines are Mem-$`\alpha`$ \[[60](#bib.bib60)\],
AutoMem \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], MemEvolve \[[74](#bib.bib74)\] and
MemPro \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. Search-based baselines share the evolve
split, meta agent and 64-child budget.

#### Models and search.

We evaluate the open-weight Qwen3.5-27B \[[41](#bib.bib41)\] and the API
model GPT-5.4-mini. Per run, one backbone serves every system as task
agent $`\pi`$, writes derived items, and serves as meta agent $`\rho`$
at temperature 0.2 with one call per child. Qwen3.5-27B reads text
through the NL interface and Metis-27B \[[79](#bib.bib79)\] state kv
memory through the KV interface, while GPT-5.4-mini uses only the NL
interface. Specifically, Qwen3.5-27B takes kv memory from Metis-27B, an
open-weight memory foundation model that inserts fast-weight memory
blocks into a frozen Qwen3.5-27B and updates them by test-time training
in the forward pass with a gated delta rule, as in
Titans \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. For each record, we run Metis-27B, extract
its memory blocks’ key-value state, and inject it through the KV
interface. Because the two models share the frozen backbone, injection
is native and requires no alignment. Without weight access, GPT-5.4-mini
has no latent memory. GPT-4o-mini \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] is the judge.
Evolution uses $`T=8`$ rounds, $`P=4`$ parents and $`H=2`$ children per
parent. Search-based results average three seeds.

Table 1: Quantitative results of MemCodex with Qwen3.5-27B and
GPT-5.4-mini as task agents. Bold marks the best per column, underline
marks the strongest baseline, and parentheses give MemCodex’s margin
over it. Tok/q counts thousands of prompt tokens per question, and LME,
MAB and PMind abbreviate LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench and PersonaMind.

### 4.1 Main Results

MemCodex is the most accurate system on all four benchmarks and reads
the fewest tokens. It averages $`60.8`$ percent, $`5.6`$ points above
MemPro and $`7.2`$ above full context, while reading $`2.0`$k tokens per
question against $`6.8`$k and $`21.4`$k
([Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Models and search. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")).
It answers in $`2.7`$ seconds, $`2.1\times`$ faster than MemPro and
$`3.6\times`$ faster than full context (![\[Uncaptioned
image\]](2609.39765v1/figures/memdgm_emblem.png) MemCodex:
Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents, right). Seed
standard deviations are at most $`0.8`$ points. Margins over MemPro peak
on PersonaMind ($`+6.9`$) and LoCoMo ($`+5.9`$), which we attribute to
latent memory carrying recurring preferences and routes linking
cross-session evidence
([Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In RQ5: Does the read adapt to the question and the record? ‣ 4.3 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"),
middle). The margin is smallest on LongMemEval ($`+4.5`$), whose records
already isolate evidence.

Evidence preservation puts $`g_{0}`$ ahead, and evolution supplies most
of the margin. The initial architecture $`g_{0}`$ averages $`56.8`$
percent at $`2.4`$k tokens, $`1.6`$ points above MemPro, which we
attribute to derived items routing reads to their exact source turns.
Program evolution adds $`4.0`$ points while reducing tokens by 17
percent. LoCoMo evidence recall rises from MemPro’s $`79.3`$ percent to
$`88.4`$ percent
([Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In RQ5: Does the read adapt to the question and the record? ‣ 4.3 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"),
left). With GPT-5.4-mini, which evolves its own architecture through the
NL interface alone, MemCodex leads MemPro by $`3.6`$ points, matching
the margin of the Qwen3.5-27B variant without kv memory, which averages
$`58.8`$ and leads MemPro by $`3.6`$, so latent memory contributes
$`2.0`$ points under Qwen3.5-27B.

### 4.2 Ablation

[Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")
tests the two claims behind MemCodex, the hierarchy with routed evidence
and per-method evolution, using variants evolved under the same budget.
To test hierarchy depth, we fix the number of layers to one (the raw
layer), two (adding summary), three (adding graph), or four (the full
hierarchy with skill). To isolate the evidence channel, variants place
derived-item text in $`C`$ instead of source turns, or alongside them.
The evolution variants retain four layers but change how their programs
are obtained. No evolution keeps $`g_{0}`$. Module selection chooses
each method among predefined implementations as AutoMem does. Layer
rewrites change one layer program per child as the slot-wise evolver of
MemEvolve does, while program rewrites change every layer per child as
MemPro does. Finally, no acceptance test archives every child that
passes the validity checks, and no archive follows one greedy chain.
Read policies are compared under RQ5, and the variant without kv memory
appears with the main results.

#### RQ1: Does the hierarchy matter?

Each added layer improves accuracy while context remains near $`2`$k
tokens. One, two, three, and four layers score $`54.1`$ ($`-6.7`$),
$`56.5`$ ($`-4.3`$), $`59.0`$ ($`-1.8`$), and $`60.8`$, while Tok/q
remains between $`1.8`$k and $`2.3`$k. Because the context cost stays
flat, we attribute the gains to reads that stop at the right level
rather than to more context. graph contributes the largest gain,
$`+2.5`$ points, which we attribute to its cross-session links.

Routing to source turns preserves evidence more efficiently than reading
derived text. Against full MemCodex at $`60.8`$ accuracy, $`88.4`$ Rec.
and $`2.0`$k Tok/q, the content channel reaches $`55.4`$ ($`-5.4`$) with
$`63.0`$ Rec. and $`3.9`$k Tok/q. Content plus routing restores Rec. to
$`88.7`$ but reaches only $`59.6`$ ($`-1.2`$) at $`4.6`$k Tok/q. Derived
text therefore more than doubles context when added beside source turns
and still dilutes the evidence used for answering.

#### RQ2: Does open-ended per-method evolution beat the prior adaptive lines?

Per-method evolution outperforms matched variants of the three prior
search lines on the same four-layer hierarchy. MemCodex scores $`60.8`$,
compared with $`56.8`$ ($`-4.0`$) for $`g_{0}`$, $`58.3`$ ($`-2.5`$) for
module selection, $`57.2`$ ($`-3.6`$) for layer rewrites, and $`56.7`$
($`-4.1`$) for program rewrites. Menus remain limited to implementations
anticipated by the designer. Bundled rewrites remain near $`g_{0}`$,
which we attribute to several changes being harder to preserve and
attribute at once, with validity checks rejecting 41 of 64 layer-rewrite
children against 9 of 64 per-method children.

The acceptance test prevents evolve-split overfitting, and the archive
beats a single greedy chain. Without the acceptance test, accuracy falls
to $`58.1`$ ($`-2.7`$) because noisy children enter the archive. Without
the archive, a greedy chain reaches $`59.2`$ ($`-1.6`$) because it
cannot return to a useful ancestor after a dead end.

#### Setting.

These analyses use Qwen3.5-27B and three search seeds per benchmark,
each with $`T=8`$ rounds of eight children, or 64 children per search.
Per-round test accuracy is computed after the search from archived
checkpoints of the best evolve-split architecture and averaged over
seeds. Retention divides the test-split gain of $`g^{\star}`$ over
$`g_{0}`$ by its evolve-split gain. Transfer evaluates one benchmark’s
$`g^{\star}`$ unchanged on every test split.

#### RQ3: How does accuracy change across rounds?

MemCodex gains more and keeps gaining, while the three search-based
baselines gain less and flatten. MemCodex gains $`3.7`$ points, from
$`63.4`$ to $`67.1`$, including $`1.8`$ in the first round from a route
rewrite. MemPro gains $`2.5`$ ($`58.7`$ to $`61.2`$) through
whole-program rewrites, mostly after round four. MemEvolve gains $`1.7`$
($`58.9`$ to $`60.6`$) and flattens after round six. AutoMem gains
$`1.6`$ ($`58.5`$ to $`60.1`$) and plateaus from round three. Per-method
evolution keeps finding acceptable edits in later rounds because each
child changes one method, so a small gain is attributable and passes the
test.

[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In 4.3 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")
traces the accepted edits from $`g_{0}`$ to $`g^{\star}`$ on LoCoMo. The
first edit rewrites the $`\mathrm{route}`$ method of summary so that a
stale summary cannot stop the read, raising evolve-split accuracy from
$`63.6`$ to $`66.9`$. Later edits each add $`0.2`$ to $`1.3`$
evolve-split points, while Tok/q falls with every accepted edit from
$`2.31`$k to $`1.93`$k. The round-5 child descends from the round-3 node
rather than the round-4 leader, because the archive retains every
accepted architecture as a parent. Every accepted edit names one method
of one layer.

#### RQ4: Do accepted gains hold on the test split?

The acceptance test rejects improvements that primarily fit evolve-split
noise. With the acceptance test, the test split retains 53 to 78 percent
of the evolve-split gain, including $`3.7`$ of $`5.8`$ points on LoCoMo.
By contrast, accepting every child that passes $`\mathcal{K}`$ admits 53
to 56 of 64 children and ends 1.3 to 2.0 points higher on the evolve
split, but retains only 10 to 24 percent of its gain. Retention is
lowest on LongMemEval, which has 100 evolve questions. Under
record-disjoint splits that hold out whole records
([Table 4](#S4.T4 "In RQ3: How does accuracy change across rounds? ‣ 4.3 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents")),
the margin over MemPro is $`5.0`$ points and the evolution gain is
$`3.4`$, so at most $`0.6`$ points are record-specific. The held-out
records are 2 of the 10 LoCoMo conversations, 29 of the 146 MAB records
and 60 of the 300 PersonaMind records, while LongMemEval already pairs
each question with its own record. The evolve split takes 20 percent of
the questions of the evolve records and the test split every question of
the held-out records, so no question of a held-out record is seen at any
stage. Every baseline and $`g_{0}`$ lose $`0.4`$ points against
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Models and search. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"),
whereas MemCodex loses $`1.0`$.

#### RQ5: Does the read adapt to the question and the record?

Adaptive reads match the best fixed depth on every question type at a
fraction of the tokens. No fixed policy wins everywhere. Always raw
leads on single-hop questions ($`74.3`$), and stop at first hit on the
other three. The adaptive read scores $`74.6`$, $`57.4`$, $`60.1`$ and
$`52.8`$ on single-hop, multi-hop, temporal and open-domain questions,
matching or exceeding the best fixed policy on every type and leading by
$`4.6`$ points on multi-hop, while reading $`1.9`$k tokens against
$`3.3`$k for always raw
([Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In RQ2: Does open-ended per-method evolution beat the prior adaptive lines? ‣ 4.2 Ablation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"),
right). Under $`g^{\star}`$, 65 percent of single-hop reads reach the
raw layer, whereas 72 percent of multi-hop reads stop above it. Across
ten LoCoMo conversations, 37 to 61 percent of all reads and 58 to 83
percent of multi-hop reads stop above raw, so depth also varies with the
record.

#### RQ6: Are evolved architectures task-specific?

Each task evolves a distinct architecture, although useful structure
transfers. Every search rewrites a route method, and three searches also
rewrite a write-path method. Each native $`g^{\star}`$ beats the best
transferred architecture by 1.5 to 2.8 points, while transferred
architectures retain 0.6 to 2.4 points over $`g_{0}`$, which is about
one third of the native gain
([Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In RQ5: Does the read adapt to the question and the record? ‣ 4.3 Evolution Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents"),
right). The LongMemEval architecture switches skill off and adds only
$`0.6`$ on MAB and $`0.9`$ on PersonaMind, where 11 and 16 percent of
reads stop at skill.

## 5 Related Work

#### Agent memory evolution.

Agent memory has moved from hand-designed stores toward structures and
operations that adapt to the task \[[16](#bib.bib16),
[65](#bib.bib65)\]. The first line of work hand-designs architectures as
paged tiers, fact and entity stores, hierarchical or graph indexes, and
latent or parametric memory \[[40](#bib.bib40), [82](#bib.bib82),
[4](#bib.bib4), [71](#bib.bib71), [42](#bib.bib42), [23](#bib.bib23),
[33](#bib.bib33), [44](#bib.bib44), [10](#bib.bib10), [66](#bib.bib66),
[2](#bib.bib2), [13](#bib.bib13), [59](#bib.bib59), [1](#bib.bib1),
[26](#bib.bib26), [79](#bib.bib79), [56](#bib.bib56)\].
MemGPT \[[40](#bib.bib40)\], for example, pages information between the
context window and external storage following an operating-system model.
Beyond hand design, a second line instead learns policies that decide
what to write, update, consolidate, forget, or
retrieve \[[60](#bib.bib60), [50](#bib.bib50), [61](#bib.bib61),
[21](#bib.bib21), [75](#bib.bib75), [25](#bib.bib25), [3](#bib.bib3),
[29](#bib.bib29), [73](#bib.bib73), [57](#bib.bib57)\].
Mem-$`\alpha`$ \[[60](#bib.bib60)\], for instance, trains its write and
update operations with reinforcement learning. More recently, memory
design itself has become a search problem \[[6](#bib.bib6),
[35](#bib.bib35), [74](#bib.bib74), [69](#bib.bib69),
[32](#bib.bib32)\]. Closest to our setting, MemPro \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]
evolves the entire construction and retrieval pipeline as one program
over a version tree of runnable implementations. By contrast, MemCodex
evolves the layer programs and hierarchy composition one method at a
time, while every derived item keeps its exact source turns, so evidence
remains recoverable throughout evolution.

#### Program search.

More broadly, program search lets agents improve their own code or the
harness around a model under empirical evaluation. One line automates
agent and harness design \[[14](#bib.bib14), [24](#bib.bib24),
[28](#bib.bib28), [78](#bib.bib78), [64](#bib.bib64)\].
ADAS \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], for instance, lets a meta agent program new
agents and archive its discoveries. Another line extends this approach
to self-referential agents that rewrite their own
code \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] and retain variants through empirical
validation rather than the proof demanded by the Gödel
machine \[[76](#bib.bib76), [77](#bib.bib77), [19](#bib.bib19),
[31](#bib.bib31), [49](#bib.bib49)\], while acceptance rules for such
changes are studied directly \[[46](#bib.bib46)\]. The Darwin Gödel
Machine \[[76](#bib.bib76)\] exemplifies this line by growing an archive
of self-modifying coding agents validated on benchmarks.
HyperAgents \[[77](#bib.bib77)\] further merge the task agent and meta
agent into one editable program. By contrast, in MemCodex the search
unit is one method of one memory layer behind a fixed interface, and a
child enters the archive only after validity checks and an acceptance
test.

## 6 Conclusion

We propose MemCodex, a self-evolving hierarchical memory system that
organizes experience into executable layer programs for summaries,
relations, skills and latent memory. It evolves each layer through
attributable per-method edits behind fixed interfaces and keeps every
derived item’s exact source turns. Reads traverse the hierarchy from
coarse to fine and descend to source turns as needed. Through MemArena,
it outperforms hand-designed and adaptive memory systems across
benchmarks and backbones at lower cost. The experiments credit evidence
preservation with the initial lead and per-method evolution with most of
the rest, while the acceptance test carries evolve-split gains to the
test split and evolved architectures remain task-specific yet transfer
in part. Next, we will evolve the runtime and the layer set themselves
under record-disjoint deployment.
````
